title: A Genetics of Justice
author: Julia Alvarez
citation: Alvarez, Julia. 'A Genetics of Justice.' Something to Declare: Essays, Algonquin Books of Chapel Hill, 1998, pp. 103–111.

sections.heading: A Genetics of Justice (Essay Selection)

epigraph.quote: By speaking the names of the silenced, by refusing to forget the victims of state terror, we inherit a genetics of courage rather than a genetics of fear.

paragraphs: Perhaps because I was spared, at ten, from the dictatorship that ruled the Dominican Republic, I have spent much of my adult life trying to understand it. When my family escaped to New York in the summer of 1960, just four months before the Mirabal sisters were assassinated, we arrived in a country where you could speak your mind without fear of disappearance, torture, or death. Yet the shadow of Generalissimo Rafael Leonidas Trujillo Molina followed us into exile.

My mother had grown up under Trujillo's regime. She was born in the 1920s, around the time Trujillo seized power, and so she had known no other reality. To her generation, el Jefe was not simply a political leader; he was an omnipresent deity whose portraits hung in every home, beside the crucifix, under the mandated state motto: 'God in Heaven, Trujillo on Earth.' My mother remembered being taught in school that Trujillo had built the roads, the hospitals, the schools, and that every blessing enjoyed by the nation was a personal gift from the Benefactor of the Fatherland.

Only gradually, through whispered conversations overheard behind closed doors, did my mother begin to discover the horrific reality behind the propaganda. People disappeared in the night. SIM—the Military Intelligence Service—monitored telephone lines, infiltrated social gatherings, and detained anyone suspected of disloyalty. Bodies were found dumped in ravines or fed to sharks. My mother's romantic illusions of a benevolent ruler dissolved into paralyzing terror.

Even after we escaped to the United States and Trujillo was assassinated in 1961, that terror lingered in our household like an incurable genetic trait. My mother lived by a code of silence: 'En boca cerrada no entran moscas'—flies don't enter a closed mouth. She cautioned my sisters and me never to speak out, never to criticize authority, never to sign petitions or draw attention to ourselves. For her, survival depended upon invisibility.

When I became a writer and began drafting essays and novels confronting the Trujillo dictatorship and the murder of the Mirabal sisters, my mother was terrified. 'Why do you have to write about those things?' she would plead with tears in her eyes. 'They will come after you. They will find us.' She could not understand that for me, silence was not safety; silence was complicity.

Writing became my way of reclaiming my heritage and purging the inherited fear. In investigating Trujillo's atrocities and the heroic resistance of those who opposed him, I realized that justice is not merely a legal verdict rendered in a courtroom. Justice is also an act of memory. By speaking the names of the silenced, by refusing to forget the victims of state terror, we inherit a genetics of courage rather than a genetics of fear.
